articles.title: Great Gaddesden farmland to be reinstated as wildlife area
articles.summary: The 30-year project aims to enhance existing grassland with specialist wildflower and herb mixes.
articles.body:
Arable land farmed by a family for about 80 years is to be restored to an orchard and wildlife area.

A 30-year project will be undertaken on a 70-acre (28 hectareS) site at Pipers Hill, Great Gaddesden, close to Hemel Hempstead in Hertfordshire and aims to enhance existing grassland with specialist wildflower and herb seed mixes.

Work is due to start later this year and will be undertaken by landowners Naturum.

Animals expected to benefit include native British species such as brown hares, hedgehogs, great crested newts, common toads and the Small Heath butterfly, a spokesperson for the company said.

The company, which buys land to restore it to nature, said a traditional orchard "that once stood on the land but was lost over a century ago" would be reinstated.

It sits within a "wildlife corridor" adjoining Highpark Wood, an ancient woodland, and the Great Gaddesden Water Meadows, home to the River Gade, a rare chalk stream, otters and water voles, it added.

The farming family will remain as long-term land managers and local children will be able to visit.

Giles Perry, co-founder of the company, said: "This land has been farmed by the same family for the best part of 80 years, and it means a great deal to us to be working alongside them as we start to bring nature back to it.

"Species like brown hares, hedgehogs and great crested newts are all found nearby, but decades of arable farming have made it harder for them to continue making their habitats here.

"Giving them the space to come back is really what this project is about."

The work is part of the Hertfordshire Local Nature Recovery Strategy (LNRS), which identified the area as a priority location for woodland, scrub and grassland recovery.

It is hoped it will "ease pressure on the River Gade which, like chalk streams nationally, has been put under stress by modern farming practices," the spokesperson added.

articles.title: 'Gargantuan' turbines could be built on farmland
articles.summary: Up to 32 turbines standing at 700ft are planned for the Suffolk, Norfolk and Cambridgeshire border.
articles.body:
An onshore wind farm, which would see up to 32 turbines built on agricultural land, has been criticised by politicians.

The proposals for Redmere Wind Farm come from Swedish company Vattenfall and would see the turbines, which are 721ft (220m) tall, built on land covering the Cambridgeshire, Norfolk and Suffolk borders.

Tristan Gale, Suffolk County Council's cabinet member for planning called the proposals "unprecedented in scale" adding the turbines "would be gargantuan and seen from miles around."

Vattenfall, owned by the Swedish state, said: "Redmere wind farm could make a major contribution to cleaner, more secure energy systems while bringing jobs and investment to the local area."

The company added the development could power nearly 220,000 homes a year, with final plans due to be submitted in autumn 2027.

The proposals, which are at a very early stage, would see the turbines and energy infrastructure built across two sites around the Shippea Hill railway station, which train operator Greater Anglia said has a "very limited train service."

Due to the size and scale of the project, it is considered a Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project (NSIP), meaning the eventual planning decision will be made by the government, rather than a local council.

The company is separately proposing the Chatteris Wind Farm near Somersham, Cambridgeshire.

But Gale, from the Reform-run council said: "Enough is enough. Suffolk cannot continue to absorb project after project without a full assessment of the cumulative impact on local people, the countryside and our economy."

He said the plans "would add further pressure to communities already facing an extraordinary concentration of major energy infrastructure."

The Sunnica solar farm, also in West Suffolk, was approved in 2024 despite local objections. Construction on the £600m project is yet to begin.

Joe Mason, deputy leader of the Conservative group on Suffolk County Council, said the project was "another hammer blow for West Suffolk and East Cambridgeshire communities."

Liberal Democrat MP, Charlotte Cane, who represents Ely and East Cambridgeshire said: "Renewable projects like this have an important part to play in our energy future, but we want to see more clarity from the developers before we can know how these plans will work in our area."

She called for local people to get involved with upcoming drop-in events to be held in Thetford and Ely in October, with more to follow in 2027.

A Cambridgeshire County Council spokesperson said: "As a host authority for the proposed scheme, the council will input into the NSIP process, and engage with Vattenfall to review their proposals as more details are made available."

Vattenfall said it is "working on design proposals and environmental work " and encouraged local people to help "shape the project from the outset."

Kevin Keable of the East of England Energy Group, which represents the energy industry across Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex, said onshore wind is much cheaper and easier to build than offshore.

He said the Redmere Wind Farm would be able to power "an awful lot of homes."

articles.title: Budget a 'step in the right direction' to help people in Jersey
articles.summary: The government releases its proposed budget with "targeted measures" to help families.
articles.body:
Jersey's government has released its budget for 2027 to 2030, with a number of targeted measures designed to help families with the cost of living.

These include increasing the number of free hours of nursery care for two to three-year-olds from 15 hours to 20 hours, and doubling the parental grant to £1,800 for families with newborns or those adopting a child.

The funding for the Health Department has increased again, from £381m in 2026 to £406m.

Last year, the Fiscal Policy Panel said Jersey was spending more than it was earning, but Treasury Minister Alan Maclean told the BBC the planned new budget was "a step in the right direction" towards correcting that.

In his foreword to the budget, Chief Minister Lyndon Farnham wrote: "For many households, the cost of living remains the most immediate concern.

"Housing, childcare and everyday living costs continue to put pressure on family budgets. Businesses are also dealing with higher costs and an increasingly competitive environment.

"We are providing practical support to help put more money back into islanders' pockets, particularly for families facing the greatest pressures."

The measures targeted to help families with the cost of living include:

Free nursery care for two to three-year-olds increasing from 15 hours a week to 20 hours

The parental grant rising from £887.25 to £1,800 for families with newborns or adopting a child

A £250 family support payment for each school-aged child in low to middle-income households in 2027

Free school meals extended to secondary school pupils on the Jersey Premium funding scheme

When asked if he thought these measures helped islanders in a meaningful way, Maclean said: "I hope so. It's a step in the right direction.

"Obviously a lot more needs to be done, but what we've sought to do is target the resources we had available to those most in need."

He also explained it was not just families measures were targeted at.

He said: "You will have the seen that the pension has been uprated by 4.7%, and we've also got the community cost bonus which helps people not in families who are typically just above the income threshold levels."

Health's spending is due to increase by £25m.

In the previous budget, the Health Department's funding was increased by £60m, something former Treasury Minister Elaine Millar said was "concerning" .

While the planned increase in health funding was less, Maclean said it was the "largest spending department by a significant way".

"We need to do some proper forensic analysis and make certain that the right money is invested to deliver the correct result for islanders," he said.

The minister also said revenues from Pillar Two, a global rate of corporation tax for multinational companies with revenues of €750m (£631m) or more, would pay towards the building of the new acute hospital.

Maclean said: "We're very fortunate to have that and we will be targeting that money at the cost of building the hospital at Overdale.

"That will reduce our need to borrow more money and it will reduce our need to use reserves."

Maclean said the budget was a "small step in the right direction" to addressing concerns by the Fiscal Policy Panel that Jersey had been spending more than it was earning .

He said: "In recent years, the government has been at an operating level of spending more than it's been receiving in income in terms of taxes and charges.

"That's not sustainable and we do need to address that.

"So we've started with this budget, but the key is I describe this as a transitional budget.

"The 2028-2030 budgetary period is where we're going to need to make structural changes to make certain that as we move forward public finances are sustainable for the long term."

States members are due to debate and vote on the budget in December.

articles.title: Sir Mark Rylance stars in updated 17th Century play set in London
articles.summary: Tartuffe Remixed is an updated version featuring African and Caribbean families in London.
articles.body:
Academy Award winner Sir Mark Rylance is starring in a "remixed" version of a 17th Century play by Moliere at the Marylebone Theatre.

Tartuffe (Remixed) is set in London with an African family about to marry into a Jamaican family and has been written and directed by Darren Raymond, with whom Sir Mark has a long working history.

Sir Mark plays the hilariously cunning Pastor Terrence Blake.

"He's the catalyst of the play. The play is really about the family, but he's a conman who comes in like any good conman in a very convincing disguise, in this case as an Anglican priest," said Rylance.

Sir Mark is the only white character in a play with an otherwise all black cast in what he describes as "an incredible meeting of two different cultures".

He added: "Because of the history of the relations of Europe and America with Africa and the Caribbean there is a rather wonderful and sometimes, no, always tragic resonance with the age of slavery."

He said: "I've learnt a lot more, but I've always loved African and Caribbean culture. I live in Brixton.

"Since I came back to England in '78, I've wanted to live in those communities. I like that culture."

Sir Mark and Raymond have found both purpose and deep friendship through working together over two decades.

They are part of Intermission Youth: Raymond as founder and artistic director and Sir Mark, first as patron, then trustee when the youth theatre became a charity.

It also marks the launch of the Intermission Ensemble, a place for the classically trained graduates of Intermission Youth to start their professional careers as actors.

This is Intermission Ensemble's first Off-West End play.

"It's a bit like Arsenal who go in and find the young football players by having a wide range of youth programmes, but then eventually have a professional team," explains Sir Mark, who is also starring in one of Raymond's plays for the first time.

Darren Raymond started Intermission Youth Theatre in 2008 as a way of helping disenfranchised young people in London feel included in society through the works of Shakespeare.

He had spent a brief period of time in the criminal justice system some years earlier and found an unexpected connection to the bard with the play Othello, during a workshop led by Rylance.

"Growing up, Shakespeare for me wasn't something I was particularly interested in, but we were looking at Othello, and Mark was doing brilliant stuff at the Globe at the time.

"He was able to come in and really introduce the text to us in a way that resonated," recalls Raymond.

"I saw a lot of myself in Othello. It was a character who was looking for love, belonging, identity. These were the very things I was searching for myself."

Many of the young people he works with are also looking for the same things, he adds.

Morenike Onajobi, a graduate of Intermission Youth, is making her professional debut as an actor, having left her full-time job in HR to do so.

She plays Kemi, the “voice of reason” in the play, and said working alongside Sir Mark meant "every single day is like a masterclass".

"Working with him and Darren combined is really fun. And they have fun, they really do."

Rylance and Raymond have plans to take the play to the West End proper, as well as to work together on more professional plays through Intermission Ensemble in the future.

I ask whether Tartuffe (Remixed) then, is not just the culmination of their work together, but the beginning of an expansion.

"I hope so!" exclaims Rylance. "I'm enjoying it so much, it's where I'm going to do my classical work."

What have they learned from each other after so many years working together?

﻿"He's a brother to me," says Raymond of Rylance, "and a lovely human being. He's a person who has changed my life, and I love him to bits."

Rylance reaches over to grasp Raymond's arm.

"He's one of the great leaders," he says.

"My faith in people is revived when I'm with Darren.

"My hope, particularly where hope is rightly placed, is with young people.

"He's just got enormous gifts and on top of it all a sense of humour."

Tartuffe (Remixed) runs at the Marylebone Theatre till the 24 October.

articles.title: Chorley Apprentice star's pie shop closure prompts Burnham reply
articles.summary: Paul Bowen says a rise in employer's National Insurance was "the tipping edge" to him closing a pie shop.
articles.body:
A pie shop owner who starred in The Apprentice has told Prime Minister Andy Burnham he is closing one of his three shops because of rising business costs.

In a social media post directed at the prime minister, Paul Bowen, who owns Bowen Pies in Chorley, Lancashire, said the increase in employers' National Insurance was "the tipping edge" to him shutting the shop on Market Street, despite it taking £100,000 a year.

"We were already trying to cover everything else going up. Then the government made it more expensive to employ people," he wrote.

In response, Burnham said: "I am listening and I'm sorry it has got to the point that you need to close your doors."

Bowen, who took part in The Apprentice in 2024, said: "Look around Chorley or your home town. How many shops have "To Let" signs in the windows?"

"Years ago, this shop would tick over and pay its way. Now, with employer's National Insurance, energy bills, business rates, wages and everything else, there just isn't enough left."

On energy prices, he asked Burnham: "What are you actually doing to bring those down?".

He also asked the government to "scrap or significantly reduce employer's National Insurance for small businesses, reduce business rates, ease the VAT burden and get business energy costs down".

"Let us grow. Let us take people on. Let us have something left to put back into the business," he said.

Burnham replied: "You're right that what you are seeing in Chorley is happening across the country."

He added: "Empty shops, family businesses closing, and buildings that have been left neglected for too long.

"We've all walked past them and thought: 'Someone should do something about that.'

"That's why, yesterday, I announced that we're investing £210 million to help bring neglected high street buildings back into use - turning empty spaces into community hubs, health centres, shared workspaces, cafés and the local services people actually want to see."

He added: "I know people don't measure growth on a spreadsheet, they measure it on their high street.

articles.title: Grimsby rallies support for £3m Town of Culture bid
articles.summary: Residents asked to help shape Grimsby's bid to become the UK's first Town of Culture.
articles.body:
People in Grimsby are being asked to show Town of Culture 2028 judges what the town means to them.

Organisers behind the bid want people across Grimsby to share their stories and ideas as they prepare their submission for the title.

Grimsby has reached the final shortlist of four large towns, alongside Basildon, Birkenhead and Rotherham.

The final bid has to be submitted by 30 November, with the winner due to be announced in March 2027.

The winner will receive £3m for a six-month cultural programme in 2028, while two runners-up will receive £250,000 each.

Now the GY28 campaign wants local people to demonstrate community support for the bid.

Its themes include Fiery Stuff, The Catch, Edge and Step Forward.

A community event in Grimsby town centre is planned for next month with performances, activities and entertainment. It will be a chance for people to find out more about the bid and meet the team behind it.

Melanie Onn, MP for Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes, said: "Reaching the shortlist from hundreds of entries across the UK is already something we can all be proud of."

Councillor Oliver Freeston, leader of North East Lincolnshire Council, said: "This is our chance to tell Grimsby's story on a national stage. The judges need to see that this bid belongs to the people of Grimsby."

To help with the final submission three new roles have been created to develop a cultural programme in the coming weeks.

articles.title: Lives will be lost unless UK does more to combat wildfires, committee chairwoman says
articles.summary: Baroness Brown says there must be better training and planning, after a record year for wildfires in England and Wales.
articles.body:
Lives "will be lost" unless more is done to combat the increasing risk of wildfires, the chairwoman of the UK's Climate Change Committee (CCC) has said after a record number of blazes this summer.

Baroness Brown told BBC File on 4 Investigates "not enough action" had been taken in light of predictions the UK is facing longer, drier summers because of global warming.

Earlier this year, one man died in a wildfire in Gloucestershire, while 19 homes were destroyed in Stourbridge , near Birmingham, and villagers were evacuated in the Cairngorms .

The government said it was investing nearly £100m to improve national resilience capabilities, which includes piloting specially trained firefighting teams.

UK 'not prepared for the changing climate'

As far back as 2012, the independent CCC warned of "more frequent wildfires due to warmer and drier conditions".

File on 4 Investigates has seen figures from the National Fire Chiefs Council showing that 2026 set a new all-time high, with 1,350 wildfires in England and Wales, up by more than 300 on last year and more than 1,000 on 2024.

Records for the number of reported wildfires were also broken in 2022 and 2025.

Baroness Brown said the CCC, formed in 2008, has been telling the government for years that the UK is "not prepared for the changing climate". She continued: "The warnings have been there and not enough action has been taken.

"I fear that lives will be lost. We need to be doing much more education and preparation."

She said that included investing in specialist teams and equipment, but also "planning our woodlands, thinking about fire breaks" and early warning systems.

By 2050, she said the risk of wildfires could be doubled across much of the UK.

Uttam and Sandy Shiralkar are still coming to terms with the loss of their family home in Stourbridge after it was engulfed by a wildfire in August .

Sandy, a surgeon, said: "We saw the complete destruction of the house. There was no roof, no floorboards. Nothing. No-one should have this experience."

The fires started accidentally in fields in Stourbridge, where farming machinery was in use on the hottest day of the year.

The couple are now living in temporary accommodation. Uttam said: "Every loss is painful, but losing a house has got a different dimension. Coming back to normality is going to take a long time."

While the risk of wildfires is on the rise, the number of firefighters has been in decline.

Steve Wright, general secretary of the Fire Brigades Union, which represents firefighters, said more than a fifth of firefighter and control room posts across the UK – some 12,000 jobs - had been cut since 2010, which left crews dangerously overstretched over the summer.

"We had firefighters from London being mobilised to Yorkshire, firefighters from Merseyside being mobilised to Dorset," he said. "The effect, when you have wildfires happening at the same time across the UK, is there's just not enough firefighters on the ground to be able to deal with them."

Phil Garrigan, chairman of the National Fire Chiefs Council, which represents senior managers of the UK's fire and rescue services, said he welcomed the £97m investment to provide six specialist firefighting teams to work across the UK.

But he insisted more money was needed to boost aerial firefighting capability and improve specialist equipment for firefighters. He said: "The money has to be there, otherwise we'll be going into 2027 and 2028 with a likely occurrence that we'll see what we've seen in 2026, which is 50 plus homes lost and families devastated by the impacts of wildfire. We've got to get ahead of that."

State-of-the-art equipment such as dedicated off-road vehicles will be bought as part of the £97m investment, which the government said was funding the biggest upgrade to national resilience for 20 years.

articles.title: Kanpur plane crash: No distress call, flight-monitoring gaps emerge in AAIB probe
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) has found that Garg Aviation did not fully follow required flight-monitoring procedures
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) has found that Garg Aviation did not fully follow required flight-monitoring procedures before its training aircraft crashed near Kanpur on August 27, killing an instructor and a trainee pilot.The seven-page preliminary report also recommends that the Directorate General of Civil Aviation issue clearer guidelines on how Flying Training Organisations should monitor flight data.The Tecnam P2006T twin-engine aircraft crashed near the Ganga Barrage less than 20 minutes after taking off from Kanpur's civil aerodrome. The 39-year-old instructor and 28-year-old trainee were killed.No records of flight-data checksAAIB said Garg Aviation told investigators that it carried out random checks of data from the aircraft's Garmin system. However, the operator could not provide records of those checks and did not have a Standard Operating Procedure explaining how the monitoring was conducted or what limits would trigger further action."When queried on flight data monitoring, the FTO stated that random monitoring of Garmin data was being carried out; however, no records of such monitoring were maintained, and there was no SOP defining how the monitoring was conducted or what exceedance limits were considered for it," AAIB said.The Garmin data card acts as a type of flight-data recorder for small aircraft. AAIB said interim safety recommendations were necessary and called for stricter compliance with flight-data monitoring requirements."Further, DGCA may issue specific guidelines detailing the procedure to be followed for flight data monitoring, which shall be made part of the TPM," the probe agency said. TPM refers to the Training and Procedure Manual.Aircraft stopped responding after final radio callThe aircraft, registered as VT-NBV, took off at around 11.11 am on August 27. About 14 minutes later, it made a radio call saying operations were normal and that it would contact the controller again after 10 minutes.That call never came."No further call was received from VT-NBV thereafter. The RT controller attempted to contact VT-NBV but received no response," AAIB said.The aircraft had no distress call before the crash. Garg Aviation was informed at around 12.10 pm that the plane had force-landed in the Ganga Barrage area, after which the company's team went to the site.AAIB said local residents had reported the crash through the 112 emergency helpline. Police and ambulance teams reached the site and took both occupants to a hospital in Kanpur, where they were declared dead.Engines and flight data being examinedInvestigators have recovered the Garmin data card from the wreckage and downloaded its information for analysis. Both engines have also been recovered and quarantined for detailed examination."Both engines have been retrieved and quarantined for further detailed examination. The investigation team is coordinating with the OEM for further examination," it said. OEM refers to Original Equipment Manufacturer.The investigation also involves Italy's ANSV and the US National Transportation Safety Board, which have each appointed an accredited representative. articles.title: In 1977, a Canadian student lost his class ring in the Barbados surf; 47 years later, a metal detectorist recovered it from the ocean and traced him down
articles.summary: A Canadian university graduate's long-lost gold signet ring was recovered after 47 years by a diver in storm recovery efforts. The ring, lost during a family excursion in 1977, was successfully returned to Frederick Morgan Perigo with the help of McMaster University.
articles.body: After nearly half a century at the bottom of the ocean, a Canadian university graduate’s lost gold class ring has been returned to him. Frederick Morgan Perigo lost the class ring back in 1977 and now it has been successfully retrieved. The reunion was made possible by Alex Davis, an enthusiast for lost items who found the ring while scanning the seabed with a metal detector. The discovery eventually set off an international tracking effort to return the heirloom back to its original owner.The separation occurred during a family excursion to the ocean with his wife, and their two young sons. While wading into the water, a sudden powerful wave knocked his youngest son off balance. As Perigo jumped to the boy's rescue, the ring inadvertently slipped from his hand. Perigo said in an official statement that he never had time to react before the ring was gone. He and his family searched the water for it in the moments after, according to CBS News, but had no luck and assumed at the time it was lost for good.A post-hurricane recovery lead to the discoveryThe storm that may have possibly exposed the ring wasn't a minor squall. According to the National Hurricane Center's report, Hurricane Beryl was the earliest record of a Category 5 hurricane in the Atlantic basin. Subsequently, Barbados was put under a hurricane warning as the storm passed through the Windward Islands in July 2024. Davis has theorized that this violent storm activity had washed away the coastal sediments, ultimately laying bare years of submerged items under the sand including the graduate's long-lost memento.“So areas where it was like a beautiful sandy beach, suddenly you can see all these rocks exposed,” Davis explained. “With that sort of in mind, I was like right, are there some areas now I want to go to where they seem like a lot of sand has been pulled out?”While scanning through an area littered with vintage coins dating back to the 1970s and 1980s, Davis’s underwater detector triggered an alert, prompting him to dig through dead coral and rocks before he saw the flash of gold. Despite having been vulnerable to shifting sands and seawater for 47 years, the ring’s structural framework remained intact. Upon inspecting his find, the diver noticed three identifying markers: Perigo’s school name, the graduation year of 1965, and his initials, “FMP”.An unexpected package on a birthdayIn order to locate the owner of the ring, Davis wrote a digital message along with pictures of the jewelry to the administrative staff at McMaster University in Hamilton. The task was complicated by the fact that in the university's alumni database Perigo was registered under his middle name, Morgan, instead of "F," which his initials on the ring suggested. Upon receiving the inquiry Laura Escalante, an alumni officer, started an extensive search of enrolled students from the institution's records dating back to the mid-1960s. Escalante successfully cross-referenced the clues from the ring until finally landing on Frederick Morgan Perigo, a mathematics major.Once a direct contact was established by the University, following Perigo’s verification on exact circumstances of his loss, Escalante connected him to Davis. Davis organised an international FedEx delivery from Barbados to have the long-lost keepsake returned to its owner. The package arrived in the hands of Perigo on the day before his birthday, completing a full circle of forty-seven-years. The unexpected timing of the arrival turned the retrieved memento into a celebratory birthday present for the Canadian resident, who was deeply moved by the collaborative efforts of his alma mater and the recovery diver.You use AI every day. articles.title: His father earned around $7 a month; decades later, Lei Jun built a tech company and a $20 billion-plus fortune: The story of the man behind a Chinese tech giant
articles.summary: Lei Jun, the founder, chairman and CEO of Xiaomi grew up in a modest family in China, studied computer science at Wuhan University and went on to build
articles.body: Lei Jun, the founder, chairman and CEO of Xiaomi grew up in a modest family in China, studied computer science at Wuhan University and went on to build one of the world’s best-known technology companies. His father was a teacher who earned about $7 a month in the early 1980s, according to TIME magazine. Decades later, Jun would become a billionaire whose fortune was estimated at over $20 billion by Forbes in September 2026.But Lei Jun's story is not only about his wealth. One of the most interesting parts of his journey goes back to his university years, when he received a 2,000-yuan scholarship and made a promise to himself that he would repay the help one day. More than three decades later, he returned to his alma mater, Wuhan University, with a 1.3-billion-yuan donation, worth about $182 million at the time.His father earned $7 a monthLei Jun was born in December 1969 in Xiantao, Hubei province, China, and grew up in a modest family. As reported by TIME magazine, his father was a teacher who earned about $7 a month in the early 1980s. The detail has since become one of the most frequently cited parts of Lei's early-life story. Lei developed an interest in electronics when he was young. His curiosity eventually took him to Wuhan University, where he enrolled in computer science in 1987. In his 2023 speech at Wuhan University, Lei said, “I grew up in an ordinary family in a county town. When I was studying at Wuhan University, my family had a heavy burden, and I made up my mind to rely on myself to survive.”He finished four years of university credits in two yearsLei graduated from Wuhan University in 1991. According to the official website of his company Xiaomi, he received his bachelor's degree in computer science that year. Lei completed all the credits required for a four-year undergraduate course in just two years. His university years were also financially difficult. Lei once recalled that his family carried a heavy financial burden while he was studying and that he was determined to support himself. He worked hard academically and applied for scholarships. One of them would stay in his memory for decades.The 2,000-yuan scholarship he never forgotAccording to the official website of Wuhan University, Lei received a 2,000-yuan scholarship while he was a student. He described it as the university's highest scholarship at the time and recalled being deeply moved when he received it. “I was particularly touched,” Lei said. “I still clearly remember that when I was on the podium receiving the award, I secretly vowed: when I have the ability, I will return it tenfold, a hundredfold, or ten thousandfold.” That promise became important much later in his life.After graduating, Lei began working in the technology industry. According to Xiaomi's official profile, he joined Kingsoft in 1992 and went on to hold several senior positions at the software company. He also founded the online retail platform Joyo.com, which was acquired by Amazon in 2004. But his biggest business venture was still ahead.At 40, Lei Jun founded XiaomiIn April 2010, Lei founded Xiaomi. Born in December 1969, he was 40 at the time. Xiaomi initially focused on smartphones, but the company later expanded into a much broader technology ecosystem. The company also grew into one of the world's major smartphone makers. Lei's personal wealth rose alongside Xiaomi's growth. Forbes' profile listed his real-time net worth at $20.3 billion as of September 29, 2026.Lei did not wait until he became a billionaire to give back to his university. According to Wuhan University, six years after graduating, in 1997, Lei made his first donation to the institution. He was 27 at the time and earning about 4,000 yuan a month. He established a scholarship at the university, initially called the Tengfei Scholarship and later known as the Lei Jun Scholarship. His contributions continued for the next 26 years. Wuhan University says he subsequently supported several projects, including the Lei Jun Scholarship, the Lei Jun Science and Technology Building and a fund related to the Covid-19 response. His earlier donations to the university totalled about 130 million yuan.Then came the 1.3-billion-yuan donationOn November 29, 2023, Lei made his biggest contribution to Wuhan University. According to the university, he donated 1.3 billion yuan in cash to his alma mater, making it the largest single individual donation in the university's history at the time. Forbes later reported the donation as about $182 million. For Lei, the donation was also the fulfilment of a promise he had made as a student. “From the beginning of my repayment journey 26 years ago, today I have finally fulfilled my wish,” he said.Lei has also spoken about why he chose to build Xiaomi after years in the technology industry. In a 2015 commencement speech at Wuhan University, he said: “I cannot have regret in life regardless of success and failure.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Satellite images show Gaza in ruins three years into Israel’s genocidal war
articles.summary: Google Maps images show scale of Israel’s destruction of Gaza, where more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed.
articles.body:
Newly updated Google Maps satellite imagery shows the scale of destruction across the besieged Gaza Strip nearly three years into Israel’s genocidal war.

With neighbourhood after neighbourhood reduced to rubble and little left but the faint outlines of main roads, it is now almost impossible to tell one part of Gaza from another. Farmland has been charred, and centuries-old places of worship have been damaged or wiped from the landscape.

A recent assessment by the United Nations Satellite Centre (UNOSAT) found that the number of destroyed structures across Gaza has increased by 9 percent since a “ceasefire” took effect nearly a year ago. Overall, about 82 percent of structures in Gaza, roughly 200,000 buildings, have been damaged, and about two-thirds of those have been destroyed, according to the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA.

Using satellite images recently released on Google Maps, Al Jazeera compared Gaza before the war with today, from Rafah in the south to North Gaza. The images of Rafah were captured this year while those of northern Gaza date from 2025 and 2024. Drag the slider to the left to see what remains of some of Gaza’s neighbourhoods.

Rafah, Gaza’s southernmost city, became a major refuge for Palestinians displaced from across Gaza, but about one million people were forced to flee the area after Israeli military operations began there in May 2024. Most had already been displaced multiple times and were forced to move towards Khan Younis, a city just north of Rafah, and Deir el-Balah in central Gaza as UNRWA shelters in Rafah were emptied.

In western Rafah, the once densely populated Tal as-Sultan neighbourhood has been almost entirely wiped out. Satellite images showed little more than sand where homes once stood.

Al-Mawasi, once a sparsely populated coastal strip of sand and farmland stretching along the coast of the Rafah and Khan Younis governorates, was declared a “humanitarian zone” by Israel early in the war. It told displaced Palestinians to seek safety there. In May 2024 as Israel prepared to invade the city of Rafah, then-US President Joe Biden warned: “If they go into Rafah, … I’m not supplying the weapons.” Israel went ahead with the operation, pushing hundreds of thousands more people into al-Mawasi, which it has since bombed repeatedly.

The latest satellite images show the once largely empty area now covered in tents and packed with families who have nowhere else to go.

Khan Younis recorded the highest number of damaged structures of any governorate in UNOSAT’s October 2025 assessment with 51,885 structures. The governorate was also one of Gaza’s main agricultural hubs, and Khan Younis has recorded the largest total area of damaged cropland in the Gaza Strip. The Indonesian Istiqlal Mosque in the Ma’an area of Khan Younis was destroyed during the war after being reopened less than two years earlier.

Gaza governorate recorded the second-highest number of damaged structures in UNOSAT’s October 2025 assessment at 51,530 with 41,663 in Gaza City alone.

Among the worst-hit sites has been Gaza City’s port, the heart of a fishing industry that once supported about 110,000 people. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization said the port has been severely damaged and most of its fishing boats destroyed.

The North Gaza governorate had the highest proportion of damaged cropland in the Strip with 94 percent damaged by July 2025, according to the UN’s Office of Humanitarian Affairs. During the war, Beit Lahiya, Jabalia and other communities in the north were subjected to repeated Israeli military operations, forced displacements and severe restrictions to humanitarian aid. Jabalia refugee camp, the largest of Gaza’s eight camps, has been destroyed with satellite images showing entire blocks reduced to rubble.

Since Israel’s war on Gaza began on October 7, 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and more than 175,000 have been injured. The true toll is likely higher because many people are still missing beneath the rubble. Since the October “ceasefire” last year, more than 1,400 people have been killed and almost 5,000 injured.

articles.title: Pitru Paksha 2026: Do Not Make These Mistakes During Shradh, Tarpan, and Pind Daan
articles.summary: During Pitru Paksha 2026, people will remember their ancestors by performing Shradh, Tarpan, and Pind Daan.
articles.body: During Pitru Paksha 2026, people will remember their ancestors by performing Shradh, Tarpan, and Pind Daan. We do these things out of respect for those who came before us, out of gratefulness, out of duty to our family.Tradition also says the way these ceremonies are performed matters. Carelessness, haste or casualness in its observance could detract from its spiritual meaning.Do Not Treat Shradh Like a Routine CeremonyThe people do the ritual because they are supposed to. When you do Shradh, be sincere and remember.Keep the focus on the person for whom you are performing the rite. If you turn the event into more of a social gathering or rush through it, you can lose the spiritual and emotional meaning.Avoid Anger and ArgumentsSerenity was the norm during Pitru Paksha in the past. It is better to avoid family fights, rude words and arguments during the Shradh.The tension can make it hard to focus on what the ceremony is for. For this reason, many families try to keep the house quiet on the day of celebration.Do Not Ignore the Correct TithiShradh is usually linked to the lunar tithi of the ascendant's death. You may not want to choose a date just because it is convenient.If the exact tithi is not known, Sarva Pitru Amavasya is observed for family members whose date of death or Shradh tithi cannot be confirmed.Do Not Perform Tarpan CarelesslyTarpan is not just pouring water. It’s a memorial offering that is meant to be meaningful.You can use water, or black sesame seeds, or certain hand positions – according to family tradition. People following a priest-led method should not change steps in the middle without understanding what they mean.Avoid Wasting Food Prepared for ShradhIn many homes, food prepared for ancestor ceremonies has a special significance. It is considered impolite to cook too much food and then throw it away.Most of the time, families make simple meals. Showy, complicated presentation is still less important than respect.Do Not Forget Family TraditionsThe tradition of Shradh may vary from place to place, community to community and even family to family. The habits done in one home may not be the same as those in another.If you copy rituals from social media without consulting your family, you can confuse yourself. If the customs are not clear, people usually talk to elders or priests who know a lot about them.Avoid Making Pind Daan a Mechanical ActPind Daan is about offering symbolic food to the ancestors who have died. It shouldn't just be about ticking boxes.The ritual is performed traditionally, with humility, care and memory. During Pitru Paksha, many families visit holy places like Gaya, but the ritual is the same.Do Not Turn Pitru Paksha Into a Fear-Based PracticePeople believe even a small mistake during Pitru Paksha can cause big problems. In traditional observance, duty, respect, and remembrance are closely connected.The rituals honour the dead, not to scare people. Focus on what matters: observe family traditions, maintain your dignity, and understand the meaning of each action.Get the latest religion news and spiritual insights. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: I, WHO TOLD YOUR STORY
articles.summary: Ever since my evolution more than three centuries ago, I have been the cynosure of human eyes.
articles.body: Ever since my evolution more than three centuries ago, I have been the cynosure of human eyes. I was born in Europe in 1609 as a printed newspaper, but it was in India that I truly came into my own .In 1780, India witnessed the birth of its first newspaper, the Bengal Gazette, published from Calcutta, then the capital of British India.Little did anyone imagine that this modest beginning would herald an enduring relationship between Indians and the printed word.My arrival was received with great aplomb. I was welcomed into homes, discussed over tea and sometimes even fought over! I was, quite frankly, on cloud nine. I felt like a king because, for a long time, I had very few contenders. My first two centuries were my glorious prime. I entered households with increasing confidence and soon became almost a family member.I have had the privilege of witnessing history from the front row. World Wars, the Indian freedom movement, the advent of nuclear warfare, political upheavals, scientific discoveries, human triumphs and follies , and I have faithfully carried them all. I reported the rise of satellites, space missions and technological marvels, while also exposing human ambition, power struggles and the occasional megalomaniac.During India’s freedom struggle, newspapers became powerful vehicles for nationalist thought. Publications such as Amrita Bazar Patrika, The Hindu and Hindustan Times carried the voices, aspirations and struggles of a nation yearning for freedom. On 15 August 1947, I witnessed history being made. Newspapers across the country brought their readers the momentous news of Independence, along with inspiring messages from national leaders and photographs that captured the emotions of a newly liberated nation. I felt immensely proud to have played my small part in recording the birth of a free India.The radio was there too by then but we were friends complementing each other.Ah, those were the days!Every morning I was eagerly awaited. A newspaper and a cup of tea were inseparable companions. In many homes, the morning ritual began with someone solemnly declaring, “Where is the paper?” as though the fate of the nation depended upon locating me!I enjoyed those first thirty minutes enormously. Some merely scanned my headlines; others turned straight to the sports or entertainment pages. The serious-minded explored my editorials and thought-provoking, spiritually awakening articles. I was popular with crossword enthusiasts , Sudoku lovers , while others searched for recipes, film reviews, cartoons, weather forecasts and matrimonial advertisements. I was not merely a newspaper; I was an entire morning’s entertainment package.And then there was R. K. Laxman’s unforgettable 'The Common Man ' and ' You Said It' in The Times of India. His gentle witty satire often said more than a thousand words could.But every reign has its sunset.The massive boom of the television in the last quarter ofthe previous century gave me a staggering blow .Then the new millennium brought me a formidable rival : the mobile phone.What a tiny, smug little creature!It is astonishing that something so small can contain newspapers, television, cinema, music, shopping, banking, games, gossip and enough information to make one’s head spin. Worse still, it delivers breaking news while I am still peacefully sleeping on the printing press!I confess I sometimes feel jealous.I watch humans travelling to work, sitting in waiting rooms, walking on roads and even having meals while staring at that little screen. Their thumbs seem to have acquired a life of their own. Scroll, swipe, tap, repeat! They are perpetually connected to the world and, ironically,sometimes disconnected from the person sitting beside them.Many families have bid me farewell. Some children born in the digital age hardly know what I am. They cannot understand why their grandparents once waited eagerly for me every morning. Nor can I blame them. Children imitate what they see. When parents themselves haveabandoned me, how are the young expected to develop an affection for my rustling pages?Yet I refuse to be bitter. Change is inevitable, perhaps necessary, and must be accepted.There was a time when people carefully cut out articles from my pages and preserved them in notebooks. Decades later, those yellowing cuttings would be rediscovered with affection. I was news,entertainment,information and sometimes even a treasure chest of memories.My ageing readers still understand this. Their hands may tremble, their eyesight may weaken and their pace may slow, but many continue to hold me lovingly, page after page. For them, I am not merely paper and ink. I am a familiar companion, a link with another era.And perhaps that is why I refuse to retire.As Tennyson so beautifully wrote:“How dull it is to pause,To make an end,To rust unburnished, not to shine in use!”I may have aged, but I have no intention of becoming redundant just yet.Nevertheless , the arrogance of my youth has mellowed into gratitude. Instead of feeling threatened by every new invention, I now marvel at humaningenuity. If technology can make life easier, improve communication and open new horizons, why should I complain?My only plea is that progress should remain people-friendly, eco-friendly and, above all, humane.So here I am , older, wiser and reconciled , watching Gen Z, Gen Alpha, more specifically the AI native generation , and the generations yet unborn , inventthe unimaginable. Perhaps one day I shall become a collector’s item, a nostalgic relic of another age. Perhaps I shall survive in some new avatar.But until then, let me continue to rustle through your mornings.To my beloved human companions, I wish to repeat Browning 's timeless words :“Grow old along with me!The best is yet to be.”Let us therefore grow oldtogether with a cup of tea in one hand, a newspaper in the other and a mobile phone resting for some time somewhere nearby!So, dear humans, keep reading, keep thinking, keep discovering , and whenever you can, spare a little affection for an old friend who has been telling your story for more than three centuries.To coexist in harmony and bonhomie....that is all I wish for now !Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: LPU Phagwara: A rape rumour sends an Indian university into turmoil and empties hostels
articles.summary: Police are trying to verify whether a female student was raped at Lovely Professional University (LPU).
articles.body:
One of India's largest private universities has suspended classes after an unverified allegation that a female student was raped on campus set off protests that descended into violence.

Police say they have registered a case and are trying to verify whether last week's alleged rape at Lovely Professional University (LPU) did happen. The university has categorically denied the allegation.

Police say no student has come forward to say she was assaulted, investigators have yet to identify the alleged victim or the perpetrator, and CCTV footage examined so far has yielded no evidence of an attack.

But rumours on student WhatsApp groups led to unrest over the weekend at the sprawling 600-acre university in Punjab that draws students from India and abroad.

Founded in 2005 by a family whose business began with a small sweet shop, LPU has grown into a largely self-contained world of hostels and lecture halls, with thousands of young people living on campus.

Images and videos showed vehicles in flames, crowds filling a major highway and police wielding canes as unrest spilled beyond the university gates. Police vehicles were damaged, officers injured and parts of the campus was vandalised.

By Monday, the highway had reopened and the campus was calmer, but heavily policed.

University authorities described the claims circulating on social media as false and baseless, but it did little to reassure students with hostels emptying within hours. Key exams were postponed and students were allowed to go home.

Following demands from protesting students, police registered a rape case against "an unidentified person" and formed a seven-member special investigation team, or SIT, to investigate.

The unrest began in the early hours of 27 September, when word spread that a female student had been raped in or near one of the university's hostels a few days earlier.

The suspect was variously described - by students and in media reports - as a plumber, painter or construction worker. Some students said the assault had occurred on 23 September and accused the university of failing to act after being informed.

BBC Punjabi found that messages about the allegation had circulated through WhatsApp groups. As they travelled, crowds gathered.

Hundreds eventually spilled on to National Highway 44, a major route between Delhi and Punjab, blocking traffic for more than 15 hours. By Sunday evening, university property had been damaged, objects set alight and stones thrown at police vehicles. Videos showed police striking protesters with canes, although police later denied carrying out a baton-charge.

Behind the gates, students described a night of fear.

"We were sitting with knives and scissors," Arya, a student, told BBC Punjabi. Students had been told to lock themselves inside their rooms, she said, while people knocked on their doors. "We were just thinking that somehow this night would pass and we would get out of here."

Police later arrived and made them feel safer, she said. By the next day, she wanted to leave. "Our parents also want us to just get out of here."

Because that was among the protesters' central demands.

"The students have been demanding that an FIR [First Information Report] is to be registered, but the students could not provide us with any victim's name," senior police official Naveen Singla told the BBC.

Police nevertheless registered an FIR under India's rape law against an unidentified person. An FIR formally records an allegation for investigation; it does not establish that a crime occurred.

Singla said investigators had also begun examining CCTV footage. The preliminary search, he told the BBC, had so far shown no outsider entering a room.

"As of now, it can't be verified that rape has happened or not," he said.

But they are continuing to examine the footage.

"The campus is quite large, so we haven't been able to see all the cameras yet," Sinha told reporters on Monday. "We have initially checked the places that the students had mentioned, but we will get to the bottom of this."

It is difficult to say. What began with an allegation of rape quickly became a broader protest over security, the university's response and, eventually, the violence itself.

There was also growing uncertainty over who was on the campus. Some students insisted the demonstrations had begun peacefully and blamed outsiders for at least some of the violence. Others told BBC Punjabi of seeing masked or unfamiliar people inside the university.

"We were really scared," said Pawan, a student. "It became a complete battlefield."

Another student, Aniket Singh, said outsiders had entered a women's hostel and knocked on doors claiming to be police officers. Police have since confirmed that outsiders were among the crowds, but said they were still trying to establish who they were and what role they played.

Amid that confusion, the university's attempt to dispel the rape allegation produced a controversy of its own.

On Monday, LPU released a video of three women living in the hostel room that had been linked to the alleged assault. They said nothing had happened there and asked people to stop disturbing them.

The same students later alleged in another video that university officials had instructed them what to say, edited the recording and posted it without their consent. Those claims have not been independently verified. LPU has not commented on the students' allegations.

Another claim circulating during the protests sought to connect the alleged rape with the recent suicide of a female LPU student from Telangana state. Police say investigations into her death had already begun and there is no verified evidence linking the two cases.

For now, life on campus has been interrupted. Regular classes have been suspended for 10 days and exams postponed. Students have been asked to return home after consulting their parents or guardians.

Those who are staying have been advised to stay in their residences and avoid further unrest.

The Punjab State Women's Commission has also sought the FIR, details of the investigation and information about arrangements for students' safety.

The investigation now has two separate questions to answer: whether there is evidence of the assault that set the protests in motion? And who was responsible for the violence that followed?

Addressing the students on Monday, LPU's pro-chancellor Rashmi Mittal said she was hurt that despite the university's many channels for students to raise concerns, they had instead "believed the rumour that was spreading". She also alleged that outsiders had joined the unrest.

"I feel students can't do this," she said.

Additional reporting by Harmandeep Singh, BBC Punjabi

articles.title: Thousands of drivers strike in the Philippines over rising fuel prices
articles.summary: Transport workers blame US-Israel war on Iran for rising fuel prices as government offers free rides for commuters.
articles.body:
Thousands of drivers of informal public transport vehicles have stopped work in the Philippines in protest against rising fuel prices , prompting the government to deploy police officers and buses to help stranded commuters.

The two-day strike, organised by Piston, a transport workers’ union, began on Tuesday.

Protesters want fuel prices cut to 55 pesos ($0.88) a litre, the level before the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in February. Organisers said that at least 70,000 drivers and operators would take part in the strike.

National police spokesman Allen Rae Co said officials had monitored 11 rallies involving 275 people in Manila and that the strike had not caused a significant disruption in the capital region.

He said 8,643 police personnel were deployed to assist commuters and maintain peace and order.

The Department of Transportation said it would provide free rides to passengers on Tuesday.

In the southeastern Bicol region, the authorities sent buses to help affected commuters, the state-run Philippine News Agency reported.

Piston has blamed the US-Israel war on Iran for the rising prices. “Fuel prices will continue to rise as long as the US persists in waging war,” it said in a social media post.

It accused President Ferdinand Marcos Jr’s government and the US of making drivers suffer through the oil crisis.

Another group, Manibela, earlier staged a strike on Monday, demanding relief from rising fuel costs and the removal of the value-added tax and excise tax on fuel.

It suspended the strike on Tuesday to hold a dialogue with the Land Transportation Office. Drivers and operators “can no longer shoulder the burden of the continuous rise in fuel prices”, the group said in a statement.

The Philippines most recently increased fuel prices on August 25. The move was attributed to geopolitical conflicts and hostilities in the Middle East, which have disrupted shipping lanes such as the Strait of Hormuz and reduced global oil supplies.

In March, the country declared a national energy emergency over the price increases, becoming the first in the world to do so.

The Philippines relies heavily on imported oil, which pushes up consumer inflation and transportation and logistics costs, and cuts into the take-home pay of drivers and low-income households.

The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board, which regulates public transport, called the fare increase a reasonable adjustment.

“Rising fuel prices significantly impact not only operators but also the workers who rely on the continuous and stable operation of public utility vehicles for their livelihood,” the agency said in a statement.

Al Jazeera’s Jamila Alindogan, reporting from Manila, said drivers in the city have seen their daily wages drop from $10 per day at the beginning of the year to less than $5 now.

“Many here say the inflation is actually bleeding communities,” she said.

“The prices of goods are also steadily increasing, and it’s a crisis that’s being felt by millions of Filipinos across the country. And although the war in Iran and the events in the Middle East have actually triggered this crisis, many Filipinos say the government can no longer use that excuse for its inability to respond to the major economic needs of millions of Filipinos,” she added.
